name: Masovian Voivodeship
summary_text: Masovian, anchored by Warsaw, is the institutional counterweight to Poland's eastern resolution belt. On 6 February 2024, Warsaw's Voivodeship Administrative Court repealed the last remaining "against LGBT ideology" document in the country. Warsaw is the origin point of the progressive response: in February 2019 Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski signed a 12-point LGBT+ Declaration (security, education, culture, sport, employment; drawn up with LGBT NGOs, including an intervention hostel and school "lighthouse keeper" projects), which provoked the first anti-LGBT municipal resolution (Świdnik, March 2019) as an explicit counter-reaction. The administrative-court campaign, led from Warsaw by the national Commissioner for Human Rights and carried through the provincial administrative courts and the Supreme Administrative Court, dismantled the resolution network nationally. The unit's dark stain is historical: in May 2005 the city under mayor Lech Kaczyński banned that year's Parada Równości, and the ECtHR in Bączkowski and Others v. Poland (2007) ruled the ban violated Articles 11, 13, and 14 ECHR. This is 20 years past and has not been repeated; the current institutional trajectory is clearly positive. Score of 0.56 sits 0.04 above the national 0.52. The only unit scoring above national in this dossier; well above Małopolska (0.48) and the eastern belt (0.42–0.45), where the resolution legacy dominates and no equivalent court-repeal or declaration infrastructure exists.

sources.claim_summary: Wikipedia overview of Poland's 'LGBT-free zone' declarations: roughly 100 municipalities plus five voivodeships (about a third of the country) adopted 'against LGBT ideology' resolutions or Local Government Family Rights Charters by 2020; unenforceable but stigmatising, and widely reported as a direct reaction to Warsaw's February 2019 declaration. On 6 February 2024 Warsaw's Voivodeship Administrative Court repealed the last 'against LGBT ideology' document in Poland, and by 24 April 2025 all anti-LGBT resolutions and family charters had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order.

sources.title: The story behind Warsaw’s new LGBT+ declaration « URBACT The blog
sources.claim_summary: URBACT blog account of how Warsaw's 12-point LGBT+ Declaration was made (March 2019): drafted with local associations (activist Oktawiusz Chrzanowski, 'Love Does Not Exclude'), promising measures in security, education, culture, sport, administration and employment - including shelter for teenagers rejected by families and anti-discrimination and sex education in schools; it sparked backlash from the right-wing ruling party and the church. Warsaw's near-two million residents include an estimated 200,000 LGBT+ people.

sources.title: Bączkowski and Others v. Poland - Wikipedia
sources.claim_summary: Wikipedia case summary of Bączkowski and Others v. Poland (ECtHR, 3 May 2007): the pre-publication ban of the 2005 Warsaw equality parade by the city president (Lech Kaczyński) violated Articles 11, 13 and 14 ECHR; a landmark establishing that parade bans require a lawful, non-arbitrary basis.

sources.title: Poland’s LGBT-Free Zones: From Declaration to Repeal - LegalClarity
sources.claim_summary: Legal explainer of the declaration-to-repeal arc (2019-2025): the national Commissioner for Human Rights (Adam Bodnar) litigated from December 2019; provincial administrative courts held the resolutions violated the constitutional equal-treatment guarantee, upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court; the EU tied cohesion funding to Charter compliance (EUR 76.5bn suspended, ~EUR 136bn frozen overall), driving council withdrawals; the last zone (Łańcut) was abolished May 2025. Resolutions were 'legally meaningless' but, per the Council of Europe Commissioner, 'directly impact the lives of LGBTI people'.
